extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in classical mechanics; readers of a mechanics textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and worked examples of classical variational principles (vis viva, Gauss's principle of least constraint, Maupertuis' least action) and related concepts (force-function/potential, level surfaces) for solving problems in dynamics. Contains definitions, equivalent formulations, derivations, and multiple illustrative mechanical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of vis viva (equation of vis viva)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equation (i), the equation of vis viva, relates the work done by forces along a path to the change in the system's vis viva (kinetic energy). It can be employed to solve problems of moving bodies when the total distance traversed and the force acting in each element of distance are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in examples: rolling cylinder/sphere down an inclined plane, chain sliding over an edge. Shows that velocities acquired often depend only on vertical descent (Galileo) or on total work done. The principle may be applied even when the actual path is unknown (Euler, Daniel Bernoulli, Lagrange extended it). Example relations and derived velocities are given (e.g., rolling devices acquire only half the acceleration of a sliding body under the same circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolling-body / rolling-without-slip consequences of vis viva
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rolling body (cylinder or sphere) descending an inclined plane (no slipping), the translational velocity and rotational motion share the vis viva; the machine considered may move with only one-half the acceleration of descent that a frictionless sliding body would have under the same circumstances (for certain mass distributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: uniform cylinder rigidly joined to a massless cylinder (different radii) alters acceleration depending on R/r; for R/r = 1 acceleration g/2; for R/r → ∞ acceleration → 0. These are quantitative corrections to naive Galileo results and apply similarly to spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain-over-edge example (vis viva application)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a chain of total length l lies partly on a horizontal plane and partly on an inclined plane, the vis viva principle yields the velocity v acquired by a hanging portion x as proportional to x (i.e., velocity acquired is proportional to the space described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: with linear mass density μ, the equation from vis viva gives v = x * sqrt(g sin a / l) (equation form shown in text). Highlights that in this case the velocity is proportional to distance described, matching Galileo's law in form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work depends only on initial and terminal positions for central and conservative forces
rubrics_metrics.description: For a body K attracted towards a fixed centre C by a given law, the increase of vis viva in rectilinear approach depends calculably on the initial and terminal distances; the increase is the same if K moves between the same initial and terminal radii by any path. For several fixed centres, the change depends only on initial and terminal distances from each centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: work is computed from projections on the radius of the actual displacements; thus for central/conservative forces the work (and kinetic-energy change) is path-independent. This observation underlies analytic treatments by Euler, Bernoulli, and Lagrange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force-function (potential) and level surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(r) is the radial component of force (negative of attractive force), then the Cartesian components of the force are partial differentials of a single function of the coordinates; that function (U) is the force-function (potential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transforming vis viva into rectangular coordinates yields dU = ... and U(initial)/U(final) differences give change in work. The equation U = constant defines level surfaces (surfaces of equal work); movement on such a surface produces no work. U increases in directions forces tend to move the bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gauss's principle of least constraint (statement and definition of constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauss's principle: for a system of masses with given connections, the actual motion is such that the sum over particles of mass × (deviation from the position it would have reached if free)^2 is a minimum. The sum Σ m (deviation)^2 is defined as the 'constraint'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle includes both dynamical and statical cases (equilibrium if rest minimizes constraint). Velocities may be neglected when forming the sum for small time elements. The principle is equivalent to D'Alembert's principle and can be deduced from it; it may be used in place of D'Alembert's. Practical forms for minimization: make 2 m s^2 (or proportional forms 2 p s or 2 m y^2) a minimum, where s relates to small declination and y to acceleration. Examples show direct application to wheel-and-axle, descent on an inclined plane (recovering Galileo's y = g sin α), levers (equilibrium), pulleys, and compound pendulums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational forms of Gauss's principle (three equivalent small-time forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a small time element, the declination s (from free motion) and associated quantities lead to several equivalent expressions that are minimized by actual motion: 2 m s^2, or proportional forms 2 p s, or 2 m y^2 (where s = y t^2/2 and y is acceleration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because constant factors do not affect the minimum condition, one may use whichever form is convenient in computations. The text uses these forms in worked examples (inclined plane, wheel-and-axle, compound pendulum) to find accelerations or equilibrium conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: derive equations of motion by minimizing the constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: To solve constrained mechanical problems via Gauss's principle: express the constraint (sum of m times squared deviations) in terms of independent small variations/accelerations, apply the minimum condition (set partial derivatives to zero) and obtain relations between accelerations or reaction forces which yield equations of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated on the moving-inclined-plane example: form the expression for total declination in terms of independent variables, differentiate w.r.t. these variables and set equal to zero to recover relationships equivalent to those obtained via conservation laws and vis viva. The principle yields the same equations as D'Alembert's principle (Gauss's gives them after differentiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical interpretation of 'least constraint' as minimization of work due to deviation from free motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The minimized expression in Gauss's principle represents the work done in an element of time by the deviation of the constrained motion from the free motion. The actual motion minimizes this constraint-work compared to any other admissible motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids metaphysical overinterpretation; the minimized quantity is a measurable work-like quantity. Examples with two forces and two masses show composition and counteraction reduce or increase the constraint in predictable ways (sum of squares of forces etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence and comparison: Gauss's principle vs D'Alembert/Lagrangian forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauss's principle is formally new in expression but not in physical content; it is equivalent to D'Alembert's principle (in its Lagrangian form) and contains statics as a special case. It furnishes the same equations of motion as D'Alembert after appropriate differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first principle (D'Alembert Lagrangian form) gives equations of motion directly; Gauss's gives them after differentiation. Gauss's principle offers a different viewpoint and can be convenient in certain constrained problems, but provides no new dynamical laws beyond established variational principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of least action (Maupertuis' formulation) and critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Maupertuis' principle (principle of least action) was stated using 'action' measured as mass × velocity × space (m v s) and asserting processes minimize that action. The text critiques this original, obscure form as mixing vis viva and virtual work notions and lacking clarity about time dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications shown: (a) impacts—minimizing the change in action yields standard impact relations (inelastic and elastic) and falls under Gauss's principle; (b) lever—Maupertuis' derivation is criticized and corrected to align with Gauss; (c) optics—Maupertuis applied a different expression (m·AR + n·RB) to refraction and obtained Snell's law, but the formulation shifts meaning of 'action' inconsistently. Takeaway: Maupertuis' historical principle is useful but not a precise, standalone foundational principle as originally stated; it reduces to Gauss/D'Alembert in corrected form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conservation laws together with variational principles for coupled systems
rubrics_metrics.description: In problems where bodies interact (e.g., a mass descending on a movable inclined plane, connected masses and pulleys), one should combine conservation of momentum (or horizontal momentum) and vis viva (work/energy) or apply Gauss's minimization to obtain accelerations and reaction forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for a body P descending a movable plane of mass Q, use Pv = Qw (horizontal momentum conservation), geometry u=(v+w)tanα, and vis viva to derive vertical acceleration y. Gauss's principle provides an alternative route via minimizing the total constraint. Several methods (vis viva + momentum, Gauss, extended moment of inertia, direct force balance) are shown to be consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended conception of moment of inertia / inertia for systems with relative motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce an extended concept of moment of inertia to account for relative velocities of connected bodies; using this extended inertia yields the same accelerations as obtained by other methods in constrained problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as one of multiple methods (second/third approach) to solve the movable inclined plane example: resolving accelerations along the path, accounting for relative velocities, and using inertia-weighted accelerations leads to the same vertical acceleration y as other principles.
